US Senate Majority Leader John Thune, pictured at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, on Tuesday, ran unopposed for the Republican party's top Senate leadership post [Jim Watson/AFP]By Evan SemonesPublished On 11 Nov 202611 Nov 2026
As they prepare to lose power, Republicans in the United States Senate have re-elected John Thune to lead their party during the final years of Donald Trump’s presidency.
At a closed-door meeting at the US Capitol on Tuesday, the South Dakota lawmaker won the support of his fellow Senate Republicans – even as some had hoped to delay the leadership vote to examine what went wrong in last week’s election.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3US voters want Democrats focused on ending Iran war, lowering costs: Polllist 2 of 32026 Midterms: Blue wave or anti-establishment backlash?list 3 of 3Did Democrats save Hegseth from impeachment?end of list
“I appreciated the opportunity to have an open, honest, and transparent conversation with my colleagues today”, Thune said in a statement after the vote. “I am honored to have their continued trust and support to lead the Senate Republican Conference in the 120th Congress.”
Unlike two years ago, when he competed against two of his fellow Republicans to replace outgoing Senator Mitch McConnell as the party’s Senate leader, Thune ran unopposed on Tuesday for the role.
Senator Josh Hawley told reporters after the vote that “maybe there would be” a challenger if Senate Republicans had waited longer.
“I just think that we’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think that to just rush into this and just ratify all of the same leadership, what message does that send?” the Missouri Republican said.

A street vendor arranges 'Kaak' a Lebanese street bread in the southern Lebanese city of Sidon, Lebanon September 6, 2022. [File: Aziz Taher/Reuters]By Justin SalhaniPublished On 11 Nov 202611 Nov 2026
Israel’s war on Lebanon has damaged the country’s wheat production and harmed the lives of farmers, experts told Al Jazeera.
For the last three years, Israel has been waging a war on Lebanon, where it has occupied large parts of the south and destroyed homes and infrastructure, in what some experts have said is a deliberate effort to make the land uninhabitable.

Repeated Israeli attacks have created havoc on the country’s wheat production, particularly in the south and in eastern Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, where lands abandoned due to the impacts of war have increased to around 24 percent.
“They’re disrupting entire ecosystems,” Munira Khayyat, author of A Landscape of War: Ecologies of Resistance and Survival in South Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. “[Israel is] advancing the possibilities of drought and desertification, basically weakening the capacity of this land to hold life.”
Farmlands damaged
Since 2023, Israel has been attacking large swaths of southern Lebanon, including using chemicals like white phosphorus, in what analysts and locals said was an effort to make the ground sterile or uninhabitable. A ceasefire was brokered in 2024 by France and the United States, but Israel never stopped attacking targets in Lebanon.

Russia has blacklisted two French lawmakers and two French journalists in response to France’s expulsion of a pro-Kremlin media network commentator earlier this year.
Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said on Wednesday that lawmakers Sacha Houlie and Arthur Delaporte would be banned from entering Russia, along with journalists Paul Gogo and Ariane Chemin.

Zakharova said the ban was for the alleged “harassment” of Xenia Fedorova, the head of RT France from 2017 to 2023.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot described Fedorova as an “agent of influence” and expelled her in July.
Fedorova, who wrote for right-wing French media, slammed “censorship” against her, while Moscow for months pledged to retaliate against “persecution”.
Ordering her expulsion in July, France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nunez had accused her of relaying Russian propaganda in an attempt to attack “the fundamental interests of the nation”.
‘Foreign interference’
Moscow has long bristled against European restrictions on its state-backed media and journalists, who Brussels and many countries in the European Union have slammed as Kremlin mouthpieces.
In a post on X, French lawmaker Sacha Houlie said: “What is intended as a sanction strikes me as recognition of my work against foreign interference in France.”

He later said that Iran’s economy “continues to collapse” and predicted worsening conditions over the next one to three months.

Kenya's Health Minister Aden Duale speaks during a news conference in Nairobi, Kenya, November 11, 2026 [Monicah Mwangi/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff and APPublished On 11 Nov 202611 Nov 2026
Kenya has released its last Ebola patient and begun a 42-day countdown to be declared free of the disease.
Health Minister Aden Duale made the announcement at a news conference in Nairobi on Wednesday, more than five weeks after the country recorded its first case on October 6.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Kenya’s Ebola cases test preparedness beyond Nairobilist 2 of 3Kenya announces second Ebola death, says ‘no evidence’ of community spreadlist 3 of 3Kenya confirms eighth Ebola case amid widening regional outbreakend of list
Duale said Kenya would continue to exercise prevention measures until the December 23 date is reached.
The Ministry of Health previously expressed confidence that the outbreak was under control, noting that all nine confirmed cases were linked to the first patient’s contact list. This indicated that there had been no community transmission. The last case was recorded on October 19.
The first patient travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) through Uganda, and transmitted the virus to four family members and four healthcare workers.
The first patient and his mother died of Ebola, while the other seven patients fully recovered. The government identified 135 contacts who interacted with the first patient.
Elsewhere in the region, the number of infections continues to climb. In the DRC, the epicentre of the outbreak, 11,042 people have been infected and 5,387 have died, the government said on Wednesday.
The outbreak also spread to Uganda and Nigeria through individuals who travelled from the DRC.
